1.text:
Where Are We in Our Galaxy?

Welcome to Quarter 4! So far we've zoomed out from Earth to the Solar System, then to the Sun and the stars. Now we take the next big jump: whole galaxies, each one holding billions of stars.

This deck asks two big questions: where are we in our galaxy, and what lies beyond it? We'll find the Sun's spot in the Milky Way, weigh a giant black hole, discover matter we can't see, and meet galaxies so far away their light left before Earth existed.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can describe the disk, bulge, halo and spiral arms of the Milky Way. I can find the Sun in the Milky Way and time its orbit. I can explain how galaxies recycle elements made in stars. I can use star orbits to weigh the black hole Sgr A*. I can explain how rotation curves reveal dark matter.

I can explain how Cepheids proved spiral nebulae are galaxies. I can use Type Ia supernovae as distance markers. I can sort galaxies by shape and explain how gravity builds them. I can place the Milky Way in the Local Group and a supercluster. And I can describe quasars and what deep fields show. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.5, ES.1.3, ES.1.4, ES.1.2 and ES.1.1, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
Our Galaxy from the Side

A galaxy is a huge island of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Ours is the Milky Way, and it's about 100,000 ly (light-years) across.

Picture it from the side. In the middle is a thin disk, made of gas, dust and young stars. Puffing up in the center is the bulge. Surrounding everything is a round halo of old stars, sprinkled with globular clusters, tight balls of very old stars. The Sun is a dot in the disk.

If you could fly outside and look, the Milky Way would look a bit like two fried eggs placed back to back: a flat white part with a fat yolk in the middle.

Did you know? The Milky Way holds 100 billion or more stars.

4.text:
We Live in the Suburbs

From the Sun to the center of the Milky Way is about 26,000 ly. That puts us about halfway from the center to the edge, out in the galactic suburbs.

Seen from above, the Milky Way has a central bar of stars and spiral arms curling around it. The Sun sits in a small arm called the Orion Spur. At the very center is Sgr A* (say "Sagittarius A-star"), which you'll meet soon.

Did you know? The Orion Nebula, the star nursery from Deck 16, sits in the same arm as us.

5.text:
One Lap Around the Galaxy

The Sun isn't sitting still. It orbits the center of the galaxy at about 230 km/s. Even so, it takes about 230 million years for the Sun to orbit the Milky Way once.

That long lap is sometimes called a galactic year. Since the Sun formed, it has made about 20 laps. One lap ago, dinosaurs were just getting started on Earth.

Did you know? At 230 km/s, you could travel from New York to Los Angeles in about 20 seconds.

6.text:
Galaxies Recycle Star Stuff

Galactic recycling means stars return enriched gas to space, and new stars form from it. Galaxies are like giant recycling plants.

Follow the loop. A cold gas cloud collapses into new stars. Those stars make heavier elements. Dying stars, as a planetary nebula or a supernova, throw that material back out. The gas, now with more heavy elements, cools into new clouds, and the cycle starts again. Each new generation starts richer.

That's why astronomers sort stars into two groups. Population I stars are young, live in the disk, and are rich in heavy elements. The Sun is one. Population II stars are old, live in the halo, and are poor in heavy elements, because they formed before much recycling had happened.

7.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Find yourself on the galactic map. Where is the Sun in the Milky Way?

Is it A) in the disk, about halfway out, B) at the very center, C) in the halo, far above the disk, or D) at the outer edge of the disk? Use Slides 3 and 4 to decide.

8.text:
A Star Orbits Something Dark

At the center of our galaxy, stars are whipping around something invisible. One star, called S2, makes one lap every 16 years. At its closest pass, about 120 AU from the center, it reaches a top speed of about 7,650 km/s.

Using the size and speed of these orbits, along with other S-stars, astronomers weighed the object they circle: Sgr A*. Its mass is 4 million Suns, packed into a space smaller than Mercury's orbit around the Sun. Nothing that heavy and that small could be anything but a supermassive black hole.

Did you know? Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery.

9.text:
The First Picture of Sgr A*

A supermassive black hole is a black hole of millions to billions of Suns at a galaxy's center. For years we could only weigh Sgr A*. Then we photographed it.

8 radio dishes around the world worked together to act as one Earth-sized telescope, observing radio light at 1.3 mm. They collected data in 2017, and the image was released May 12, 2022.

The picture shows a glowing gas ring around a dark shadow. The ring is hot gas swirling around the black hole, and the shadow is where light can't escape. Its size matched a 4-million-Sun black hole, so two totally different methods agreed.

10.text:
The Outer Stars Move Too Fast

A rotation curve is a graph of how fast stars orbit at each distance from a galaxy's center. In the Solar System, outer planets move slower, because almost all the mass is in the Sun. Astronomers expected galaxies to work the same way, based on the stars and gas we see.

But that's not what they found. In 1970, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured the Andromeda galaxy and found the curve stays flat. Outer stars move about as fast as inner ones. By 1980 they had checked 21 more spirals, and all were flat.

The only way outer stars can move that fast is if there's a lot more mass than we can see, pulling on them.

11.text:
Most Matter Is Dark

The universe has about 5 times more dark matter than ordinary matter. Ordinary matter is anything made of atoms: stars, gas, planets, you. Dark matter gives off no light. We know it's there only by its gravity.

In our galaxy, the visible disk sits inside a huge dark matter halo that reaches at least 200,000 ly from the center. That's far beyond the edge of the visible disk, which is only about 50,000 ly from center to edge.

What is dark matter made of? Nobody knows yet. It's one of the biggest mysteries in science.

12.text:
Gravity Bends Light

Gravitational lensing is when a big mass bends the path of light passing near it, like a lens. Objects behind it look stretched, brighter, or doubled. Einstein predicted this in his general relativity.

The first test came at the 1919 solar eclipse. Eddington and Dyson saw starlight bent by the Sun, just as Einstein said. Today, whole galaxy clusters make arcs and copies of galaxies far behind them. Abell 370, a cluster about 4 billion light-years away, was one of the first seen lensing.

This matters for dark matter, because how much light bends tells us how much mass is there, dark matter included.

13.text:
The Bullet Cluster

The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that smashed into each other, about 3.8 billion ly away. It gave scientists a chance to separate normal matter from dark matter.

The pink shows X-rays from hot gas, which is most of the normal matter. It slowed down in the crash, like two water balloons colliding. The blue is a lensing map showing where most of the mass is. It kept going, passing right through.

So the mass and the gas ended up in different places. Most of the mass is matter we cannot see. Published in 2006, this was direct evidence for dark matter.

14.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Think about how we see the galaxy's center. Why was the first picture of Sgr A* made with radio light?

Is it A) radio waves pass through the dust that blocks visible light, B) black holes give off radio waves from inside, C) radio telescopes are closer to the center, or D) visible light is too slow to reach us? Choose, and be ready to say what's wrong with each of the others.

15.text:
Spiral Nebulae Are Galaxies

About 100 years ago, astronomers argued about fuzzy spiral clouds in the sky. Were they inside the Milky Way, or separate galaxies? The answer came from a special kind of star.

A Cepheid variable is a pulsing star whose period tells its true brightness. In 1912, Henrietta Leavitt found the rule: longer period, brighter star. If you know how bright a star really is and how bright it looks, you can figure out its distance.

In 1923 and 1924, Edwin Hubble measured Cepheids in Andromeda. His result was announced on January 1, 1925: Andromeda was about 900,000 ly away. Today we know it's about 2.5 million ly. Either way, it's far outside the Milky Way: a galaxy of its own. The universe suddenly got much bigger.

16.text:
Exploding Stars as Yardsticks

Cepheids work for nearby galaxies, but for far ones we need something brighter. Every Type Ia supernova reaches a peak brightness of about 4.5 × 109 Suns. Because they all peak at nearly the same brightness, they work as standard bulbs.

Astronomers build a distance ladder, one rung at a time. Parallax works for nearby stars. Cepheids reach nearby galaxies. Type Ia supernovae reach far galaxies, farther and farther out. Each step is checked against the one below it.

For example, the galaxy M100 is about 56 million ly away.

17.text:
Sorting Galaxies by Shape

The tuning fork diagram is Hubble's chart of galaxy shapes: elliptical, spiral, barred spiral and irregular. It looks like a tuning fork with a handle and two prongs.

On the handle are ellipticals, smooth balls of stars from E0 (round) to E7 (most stretched). At the fork is S0, a disk with no arms. One prong holds spirals, Sa, Sb and Sc. The other holds barred spirals, SBa, SBb and SBc, which have a bar of stars across the middle. Finally, irregular galaxies (Irr) have no regular shape at all.

Going from a to c, the bulges get smaller and the arms more loosely wound. The Milky Way is a barred spiral.

Did you know? The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, two small galaxies near ours, are irregulars.

18.text:
Andromeda Is Coming

The Andromeda galaxy is heading our way, closing at about 110 km/s. In about 4.5 billion years, Andromeda may reach the Milky Way.

But a 2025 study found only about a 50% chance of a merger in the next 10 billion years. If they do merge, they would become one giant elliptical, billions of years later.

Even if galaxies collide, stars almost never hit each other. The space between stars is huge compared with the stars themselves.

19.text:
Diagram: Gravity Builds Galaxies

Time to show how it all fits together. This task matches standard ES.1.3. Draw five boxes: 1, a cloud of H and He. 2, gravity pulls in. 3, the first stars. 4, a young galaxy. 5, galaxies merge.

Add arrows showing where gravity pulls in each box. Show stars returning heavier elements to the gas, like the recycling loop on Slide 6.

Finish with one line: what would the universe look like with no gravity?

20.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Now the key idea of this part. What pulls a cloud of hydrogen and helium together to form stars and galaxies?

Is it A) gravity, B) magnetism from the stars, C) the expansion of the universe, or D) heat from the Big Bang? Choose, and explain why the other three can't do the job.

21.text:
Our Galactic Neighborhood

The Local Group is our small group of galaxies, held together by gravity. It's nearly 10 million ly across.

Two big spirals rule it: the Milky Way and Andromeda (M31). A smaller spiral, M33, is the third. The rest are dwarf galaxies, small galaxies with far fewer stars, like the LMC and SMC (the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds).

Did you know? Astronomers keep finding new faint dwarf galaxies in the Local Group, so the count keeps growing.

22.text:
Our Supercluster: Laniakea

Zoom out again. Our home supercluster, Laniakea, holds about 100,000 galaxies and stretches about 520 million ly across.

Within it is the Virgo Cluster, about 50 million ly from us, with thousands of galaxies. The Milky Way and Local Group sit near Laniakea's outer edge. Across Laniakea, galaxies flow inward toward a common center, like rivers draining into one basin.

Did you know? Laniakea is Hawaiian for "immense heaven."

23.text:
The Brightest Galaxy Centers

A quasar is the blazing center of a far galaxy, powered by gas falling into a black hole. Around the supermassive black hole is a hot disk of gas, and some quasars shoot out a jet.

The first quasar identified was 3C 273, in 1963. Its light was so redshifted that it was moving away at 45,000 km/s. That meant it was billions of light-years away, so it had to be incredibly powerful to look as bright as it does.

How powerful? A quasar can give off up to 1014 Suns of light. That's a hundred trillion Suns, brighter than whole galaxies.

24.text:
Looking Back in Time

In 2004, Hubble stared at one tiny patch of sky for 11.3 days of exposures. The result was the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, showing about 10,000 galaxies in that one speck.

Because light takes time to travel, deep fields are time machines. The faintest galaxies are seen as they were billions of years ago.

Look at the red dot. Its light left under 300 million yrs after the Big Bang. It was found by Webb in 2024, just outside this field. Its light is red because the expansion of the universe stretched it.

Did you know? The Ultra Deep Field patch is smaller than a tenth of the width of the full Moon.

25.text:
Illustrate Our Cosmic Address

Remember the cosmic address from Deck 1? Now you can fill it in with real detail. This task matches standard ES.1.5. Draw six boxes: 1, Sun and planets. 2, multiple stars. 3, a star cluster. 4, the Milky Way. 5, the Local Group. 6, Laniakea.

Draw what each level holds, from smallest to largest. Under each box, write one size or distance, in AU or ly. Add arrows showing each level sits inside the next.

Last line: which force holds every level together?

26.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Time to rank the levels. Which list goes from smallest to largest?

Is it A) galaxy, star, Local Group, star cluster, B) Local Group, galaxy, star cluster, star, C) star, star cluster, galaxy, Local Group, or D) star cluster, star, Local Group, galaxy? Use your cosmic address from Slide 25.

27.text:
Exit Ticket

You've traveled from the Sun's neighborhood to the edge of the visible universe. Show what you learned.

First, sketch the Milky Way from the side. Label the disk, bulge and halo, and mark the Sun. Second, why do astronomers think galaxies hold dark matter? Third, how do Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae tell us how far away a galaxy is? Fourth, draw 3 boxes showing how gravity turns a cloud of hydrogen and helium into a galaxy of stars.

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

28.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.5: show how stars, planetary systems, multiple-star systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups fit inside one another, and how big each one is. ES.1.3: show how energy cooled into protons and early elements, and how those elements formed huge stars and galaxies. Explain how gravity pulls clouds of these elements together into stars and galaxies.

ES.1.2 is introduced here: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence like the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law and the cosmic microwave background. ES.1.1 is review: we study space by observing every kind of light with different telescopes.
